summary: Psalm 86 is a personal prayer for help from someone who calls himself poor, needy, and threatened. The speaker moves from urgent petitions to praise of God's uniqueness, asks to be taught an undivided way of life, and returns to the danger posed by proud and violent enemies. The psalm ends by asking for a visible sign of God's goodness so that enemies will see that Yahweh has helped and comforted him.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how a psalm can hold need, trust, praise, instruction, and danger together in one prayer. It also repeats descriptions of God as merciful, forgiving, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, making God's character the ground for the speaker's requests.

context.author: The heading says, “A Prayer by David.” In Psalms, such headings are ancient features of the collection, but readers differ on whether each one functions as a modern author byline, a mark of association, or another kind of collection notice.
context.audience: Psalms was gathered for Israel's worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities also adopted these prayers for public and private use.
context.date: The Psalter is an anthology formed over time; assigning one date to all its poems would be misleading. This psalm appears in Book III of Psalms, within chapters 73–89.
context.setting: The poem does not name a specific event or place. It speaks from personal distress, opposition, and dependence on God.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with repeated petitions, parallel lines, praise, and direct address to God.

outline.heading: A plea from need
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to hear, preserve, save, show mercy, and bring joy, presenting himself as poor, needy, trusting, and constantly calling.

outline.heading: Confidence that God hears
outline.note: The prayer rests on God's goodness, forgiveness, loving kindness, and expected answer in trouble.

outline.heading: God alone among the gods
outline.note: The speaker praises God as unmatched in deeds, worshiped by all nations he made, and God alone.

outline.heading: A request for an undivided heart
outline.note: The speaker asks to be taught God's way, promises whole-hearted praise, and says God has delivered his soul from the lowest Sheol.

outline.heading: Enemies and God's character
outline.note: The proud and violent seek the speaker's soul, but God is described as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.

outline.heading: Strength and a sign
outline.note: The psalm closes with requests for mercy, strength, rescue, and a sign of goodness that would show Yahweh's help and comfort.

keyVerses.text: For you, Lord, are good, and ready to forgive, abundant in loving kindness to all those who call on you.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the reason the speaker keeps calling: God's goodness, forgiveness, and loving kindness are presented as the basis for prayer.

keyVerses.text: For you are great, and do wondrous things. You are God alone.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm's praise by moving beyond the speaker's distress to God's unmatched greatness.

keyVerses.text: Teach me your way, Yahweh. I will walk in your truth. Make my heart undivided to fear your name.
keyVerses.why: The prayer is not only for rescue; it also asks for instruction and inner wholeness before God.

keyVerses.text: But you, Lord, are a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.
keyVerses.why: This verse restates God's character at the moment the speaker names his enemies, so the crisis is answered first by who God is.

themes: Threat from proud and violent enemies

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin with “A Prayer by David”?
questions.answer: The heading connects the psalm with David, but Davidic headings can be read in more than one way. Some readers take it as authorship, while others see association, dedication, collection, or reception. The chapter itself does not name a specific event in David's life.

questions.question: What does the speaker mean by “poor and needy”?
questions.answer: The phrase presents the speaker as dependent and in distress. The rest of the psalm fills that out with repeated requests for mercy, rescue, strength, and help against enemies. It is not a detailed economic report; it is the posture from which the prayer begins.

questions.question: Why does the speaker call himself “godly”?
questions.answer: In this verse, “godly” stands beside trust and servant language: “save your servant who trusts in you.” The speaker is appealing to his relationship with God, not claiming that he has no weakness or need. The same psalm still asks for mercy and help.

questions.question: Does “among the gods” mean the psalm believes in many equal gods?
questions.answer: The psalm says, “There is no one like you among the gods,” and then says, “You are God alone.” Readers may discuss how ancient poetic language about “gods” works, but within this chapter the point is comparison that leads to God's uniqueness, not equality among divine beings.

questions.question: What does the psalm say about the nations?
questions.answer: Verse 9 says that all nations God has made will come, worship before the Lord, and glorify his name. The psalm presents this as part of God's greatness, not as a narrated event happening in the speaker's immediate situation. Later Jewish and Christian readers may connect this verse with wider hopes for the nations, but the chapter itself states the worship of the nations in broad poetic form.

questions.question: What is an “undivided” heart?
questions.answer: The speaker asks God, “Make my heart undivided to fear your name.” In the flow of the verse, this means a heart aligned with God's way and truth rather than pulled in competing directions. The psalm presents it as something God must give, not merely something the speaker can produce alone.

questions.question: What is “the lowest Sheol”?
questions.answer: Verse 13 says God has delivered the speaker's soul from “the lowest Sheol.” In Psalms, Sheol is associated with the realm or depth of death, but this line does not give a full map of the afterlife. The phrase emphasizes the extremity of danger from which the speaker says he has been delivered.

questions.question: Who are the “proud” and “violent men”?
questions.answer: The psalm does not identify them by name. It describes them by what they do: they rise up against the speaker, seek after his soul, and do not hold regard for God before them. The danger is real in the poem, but the historical setting remains unnamed.

questions.question: Why ask for a “sign” at the end?
questions.answer: The speaker asks for a sign of God's goodness so that those who hate him may see it and be shamed. In the verse, the sign would show that Yahweh has helped and comforted him. The psalm does not specify what the sign should be, so readers should not fill in a particular miracle or event as certain.

glossary.def: A repeated description of God's dependable mercy or loyal kindness in this psalm. It appears in the reasons the speaker gives for trusting God.
Requests or pleas. The speaker asks God to listen to the voice of his petitions in verse 6.
God's remarkable deeds. The phrase appears in the psalm's praise of God as great and God alone.
The depth or realm associated with death in the psalm's language. The speaker says God has delivered his soul from the lowest Sheol.
